opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is honesty about what you're actually measuring. In a big organization there's always pressure for a number to go up, because the number is how progress gets communicated upward and outward. Once a benchmark becomes the target, people start optimizing for it in ways that may not reflect real capability. So responsible evaluation starts with a culture that says: we care more about knowing the truth than about looking good.

Concretely, a few things matter a lot to me.

One is contamination and leakage. With models trained on huge amounts of web data, you have to assume your test set may have leaked into training in some form. You need deliberate effort: held-out sets that are actually private, fresh evaluations built after the training cutoff, and checks for whether the model is recalling rather than reasoning.

Second is not trusting a single number. Aggregate scores hide a lot. A model can improve on average while getting worse on things users care about, or on safety-relevant behaviors. You want to break results down, look at failure cases by hand, and actually read outputs. Researchers who skip reading transcripts often fool themselves.

Third is variance and rigor. Many claimed improvements are within noise: different seeds, prompt formats, sampling temperatures. In a large org many teams run many experiments, and if you only report the best one you're effectively p-hacking. Pre-registering what you'll measure, reporting confidence intervals, and having someone outside the team reproduce results are boring but very important.

Fourth, evaluation should track what you really want the system to do. As models become more agentic, working over long horizons, using tools, interacting with real environments, static question-answer benchmarks capture less and less. Building evaluations closer to real tasks is hard and expensive, but I think it's where much of the real research value lies now. In some sense, defining the right evaluation is half the research problem.

Finally, there's an organizational side. Evaluation teams need some independence. If the people judging a model are the same people whose bonus depends on it shipping, that's a conflict of interest. You want people empowered to say "this isn't ready" or "this result doesn't hold up," and leadership that rewards them for it instead of treating them as a bottleneck.

So in short: guard against fooling yourself statistically, guard against fooling yourself culturally, and keep asking whether your measurements still match the capabilities and risks you actually care about.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that responsible evaluation is mostly about resisting the incentives that push you toward evaluating irresponsibly, and those incentives get stronger the bigger the organization is.

Let me break that down. In a large lab, an evaluation is never just a measurement. It's a signal that decides whether a project gets more compute, whether a team gets credit, whether a model ships. So the moment a benchmark becomes the thing people are judged on, it stops being a neutral instrument. People will, often without any bad intent, start optimizing for it. You see training data drift toward the test distribution, you see prompt tuning on the eval set, you see cherry-picked checkpoints. None of that is fraud, but the number stops meaning what it used to mean.

So the first requirement is separating the people who build the system from the people who decide what "good" looks like. Not completely, because the builders know where the bodies are buried, but enough that the eval isn't designed by the same person whose promotion depends on it. In practice that means some kind of held-out, periodically refreshed evaluation set that the training teams genuinely cannot see, plus someone whose job it is to say "no" when the result looks too clean.

The second requirement is being clear about what question you're actually asking. A lot of the time when I look at an eval, I can't tell if it's measuring the thing we care about or a proxy for it. For agents especially, this is hard. Did the agent solve the task, or did it exploit a quirk of the environment? Did it generalize, or did it memorize a pattern from a similar task in pretraining? If you don't write down the question before you run the experiment, you'll always find a way to read the result as good news.

Third, you need to report the whole distribution, not just the mean. Variance across seeds, failure modes, where the model breaks. In my own work I've found that the most informative part of an eval is usually the failure cases, and those are precisely what gets dropped when a result turns into a slide.

And finally, and this is maybe the uncomfortable part, you need a culture where a negative result is still a result. If the only evaluations that get surfaced are the ones that went well, then the organization is systematically lying to itself, and no amount of methodology fixes that. Responsible evaluation at scale is ultimately a management problem as much as a technical one. The technical part, we mostly know how to do. The hard part is building an organization that actually wants to know the answer.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to be clear about what an evaluation actually tells us. A benchmark score is evidence about performance under certain conditions. It doesn’t automatically tell us whether a system is useful, reliable, or safe in deployment.

For a large research organization, I would want several layers. You need reproducible experiments and careful checks for data contamination. You also need evaluations that reflect how people actually use the system, including difficult cases and the consequences of failure. For an agent, for example, reaching the right final answer isn’t enough—you should also examine what actions it took and whether those actions were authorized.

And there’s an organizational aspect. The people evaluating a model need room to report results that are inconvenient for the people building it. Otherwise, you can have very sophisticated metrics and still make poor decisions.

So I’d treat evaluation as an ongoing process: state the assumptions, measure the limitations, and keep checking whether the evidence supports the claims you’re making.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to be clear about what you’re evaluating. A model can do well on a benchmark, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it will be useful or reliable in a real application. So you need to connect the evaluation to the setting where the algorithm will actually be used: what decisions it makes, who is affected, and what happens when it fails.

In a large organization, that also requires a process where people can report negative results and challenge the evaluation itself. If everyone is optimizing for the same number, it’s easy to improve the number without improving the underlying capability. You want reproducible experiments, careful analysis of failures, and independent checks, especially when the team developing the algorithm has an incentive to show progress.

And I would treat evaluation as something continuous. Once you deploy a system, users will encounter situations that your tests didn’t cover. Responsible evaluation means learning from those cases, updating your tests, and being explicit about what the evidence supports and where there is still uncertainty.
